cim: ARTEX Demonstrates Growing Risks of AI-Powered Cyberattacks
cim_eredeti: ARTEX Demonstrates Growing Risks of AI-Powered Cyberattacks
szoveg_eredeti:
For cybersecurity professionals and businesses of all sizes, it feels like the world is on fire. For illustrative purposes, insurance broker Marsh said that in the last two weeks of May the number of cybersecurity incidents reported by its clients was 48. In the last two weeks of October, that number has more than doubled to 105.[1] This increase is being driven by using Artificial Intelligence in cyber attacks, but not in the way you might expect. It’s driven not by a massive increase in zero-day exploits discovered by a threat actor’s use of Artificial Intelligence, but by Artificial Intelligence making the exploitation of known vulnerabilities much easier and efficient. Nowhere is this dynamic more clearly illustrated than the case of ARTEX.

Cybersecurity professionals have always dealt with a familiar problem: Tools designed to help organizations test their defenses can also be used by attackers. For those who have been following cybersecurity for a while, Cobalt Strike is a good example. Originally developed for legitimate security testing, it has become a tool frequently used in real-world attacks.

Now, AI-powered penetration-testing frameworks (or “harnesses”) are raising similar concerns. These tools take automation a step further, allowing attackers to carry out multiple stages of an attack with less hands-on involvement. The harness is essentially a software layer that manages tools, memory, context, and execution that allows an LLM to act as an agent.

ARTEX, an open-source Chinese AI harness that was initially developed for penetration-testing purposes, has reportedly been used by both nation-state and financially motivated threat actors to efficiently execute cyber attacks. Its growing capabilities highlight how quickly AI is changing the cyber security landscape.

ARTEX is a harness written in Go that uses large language models (LLMs) to automate offensive security tasks. Unlike traditional tools that rely heavily on an operator to direct each step, ARTEX uses AI agents to carry out different activities with limited human involvement.

ARTEX also builds a graph of the assets and vulnerabilities it discovers. This allows its agents to use information gathered during an assessment to determine what to investigate or target next.

Automation isn’t new to cybersecurity. Security teams and attackers have relied on scripts, scanners, and penetration-testing frameworks for years to speed up repetitive tasks.

What makes ARTEX different is how it uses AI to make decisions as an operation progresses. Rather than simply following a predefined list of commands, its agents can respond to new information, adjust their approach, and continue working toward an objective with less direction from a human operator. A good example is how ARTEX responds when confronted with a CAPTCHA. ARTEX has been documented establishing an outside email account to get around CAPTCHA challenges in the wild.

Microsoft researchers described an AI-enabled attack chain that went from searching GitHub for exposed secrets to extracting data from an Azure Key Vault in approximately five minutes.

That’s a significant concern for defenders. Tasks that once required considerable technical knowledge and manual effort can now be completed much faster with the help of AI. This doesn’t mean attackers no longer need technical expertise, but it does mean the barrier to carrying out certain types of attacks is getting lower.

Although tools like ARTEX introduce new capabilities, the underlying attack techniques aren’t necessarily new. Many of the same weaknesses that attackers have exploited for years are still at the center of these incidents.

Identity security is a good place to start. Organizations should enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA), use conditional access policies, implement privileged access management, and regularly review service accounts and OAuth applications. It’s also important to monitor for unusual Microsoft Graph activity, unexpected privilege changes, and modifications to application credentials. As more business operations move to cloud platforms, monitoring identity and application activity is becoming just as important as traditional endpoint monitoring.

Third-party and supply chain security deserve attention as well. The ConnectWise incident is a reminder of the risks that come with relying on external vendors and trusted software providers. A compromise of one vendor can potentially expose multiple customer environments. Organizations should maintain an inventory of approved third-party applications, review the permissions those applications have been granted, and remove integrations that are no longer needed. Applying least-privilege access to applications and regularly auditing SaaS connections can help limit the damage if an account or integration is compromised.

Organizations should also prepare for attacks to move faster. Continuous monitoring, effective threat detection and response, regular threat hunting, and proactive vulnerability management all play an important role. Security teams may have less time to identify and contain an attack as AI makes it easier to automate different stages of an intrusion.

Ultimately, AI doesn’t eliminate the security weaknesses attackers have relied on for years. Exposed credentials, excessive permissions, misconfigured cloud environments, vulnerable internet-facing systems, and poorly managed third-party integrations remain attractive targets.

ARTEX is another example of how attackers can use existing technology in new ways. The tools may be changing, but many of the security fundamentals organizations need to get right haven’t.
